Dear Sunaina didi,
You're the only one in the family I can write this to without the whole group chat finding out. I didn't sit for the prelims this year. I told Papa at Diwali, and Chacha said, loud enough for everyone, "Three generations of officers and this girl is lost." Papa didn't defend me. Love,
Nandini

Sunday. After lunch Elizabeth, twenty, told her mother she wanted to stop going to the morning service for a while, just to think about what she herself believes. Her mother set down the plates. Counselling note, Tuesday afternoon.
Kunal arrived fifteen minutes early and sat with his bag held tight on his knees. He said his father called him "ungrateful" on the phone last night, only because Kunal asked whether he really had to take over the family printing press after his degree. He kept repeating, "They built everything for me." His voice dropped when he said none of his hostel friends get it; their parents "just want them to have any job." He showed me a notebook of stage-set sketches he has never shown at home. I did not tell him what to choose. I asked which parts of the press he actually likes. He said the smell of ink and the late-night rush with his uncle before an election. Midway, his elder sister Bidisha texted: "Papa is hurt, not angry. Come home Sunday?" He smiled for the first time. Before our next meeting he will write two lists: what he wants, and what he was handed.

Bilal had grown up in Lyon going to the mosque every Friday with his father, never missing. At twenty, at university, he started reading philosophy and asking questions he couldn't answer.
He told his father he wanted time to think about what he really believed.
His father's face closed. "After everything we gave you, you want to throw it away? You're lost."
Bilal walked back to his student room feeling like a traitor. He still loved the Friday meals, his father's voice reciting. He wasn't rejecting them. He just wanted his faith, or whatever it became, to be his own.
His friend Gabriel found him on the stairs. "You look awful."
"My dad thinks I've abandoned him."
"Have you?"
"No," Bilal said, and realised he meant it. "I just need to find out what's mine."
